source.title: Optimal Splitting of Language Models from Mixtures to Specialized Domains
source.authors: Skyler Seto; Pierre Ablin; A. Filippova; Jia-Yu Ye; Louis Béthune; Angelos Katharopoulos; D. Grangier

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests loss scaling and extrapolation in a new setting: two-stage, multi-domain pretraining followed by continued pretraining of split models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling-law fits, held-out loss-prediction errors, extrapolation tests, optimal pretraining allocations, and downstream QA results. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own loss law (power terms in N, D, Dk plus a sigmoid bias) to two-stage pretraining and continued-pretraining (CPT) runs on DCLM clusters. It tests extrapolation to held-out larger models (1.3B→2.7B) and to larger PT/CPT token budgets. This bears on V2 and on V5 (continued pretraining regime). Its allocation results concern PT-vs-CPT splitting, not the N-vs-D compute-optimal split of V3, and its QA tables mostly compare its method with baselines.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude their split-training law accurately predicts loss for larger models and token budgets than fitted, and that training at the law's optimal split point gives about 2% better zero-shot QA at equal compute. Split 2.7B models beat a pretrained 6.7B model with roughly double the inference cost. They also argue PT and CPT compute should be planned jointly.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a two-stage, clustered multi-domain training method and a custom loss law with PT/CPT terms; it is not a reproduction of the original single-stage scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported optimal split varies with total training budget and model size; the optimal pretraining fraction decreases as budget rises, while the optimal pretraining-token count rises.

fits_no_version.finding: For a fixed total budget, the loss-optimal pretraining fraction decays as the budget grows, while optimal pretraining tokens increase. The minimal useful splitting point Dsplit grows with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal PT-vs-specialization allocation in multi-domain split training shifts predictably with budget and model size.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal PT fraction is fit as a power law fs(N)=a·N^b on 100M–1.3B models and extrapolates closely to 2.7B (Appendix G.2, Fig 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal PT/CPT allocation follows a power law in model size and can be extrapolated from small runs.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal compute, split models beat same-size pretrained models by about 1.5–2% average QA. Split 2.7B averages about 0.6% above a pretrained 6.7B model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-matched split specialization beats full pretraining on downstream QA.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the listed fit or QA results. Some key loss and allocation curves are presented only in figures. The extrapolation evidence is from the study's own DCLM split-training setup, and the tested optimal-allocation trend is not fitted as a compute power law.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports phonebook memorization, two-cluster DCLM curves, Pile-domain perplexities, varying-domain-count experiments, and per-cluster MoE perplexities. These are not extracted because they report split-training outcomes without testing the loss-scaling, extrapolation, compute-optimal power-law allocation, architecture-shape, or downstream-predictability versions as defined here. Figure-only numerical values for the QA and loss curves are not transcribed.

untested.parts: No standalone power-law fit of single-stage pretraining loss in N, D or compute. The Chinchilla form is assumed as a sub-case of the custom law, not tested on its own.
Extrapolation across orders of magnitude: tested only about 2× in N (1.3B→2.7B) and within the token ranges.
Entirely untested: no fit of loss-optimal N and D against compute, and no Kaplan-vs-Hoffmann comparison.
Entirely untested: no fixed-N shape comparison.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer beyond text continued pretraining.
Downstream accuracy as a function of scale or loss across sizes; no fitted downstream trend.
No systematic test of how exponents or optimal splits change with fitting choices. Parameter bounds and identifiability are discussed only.

missing.what: Pretrained-only accuracies across 1.3B, 2.7B and 6.7B at matched compute. Most benchmarks rise with size, but BoolQ (65.78→63.12) and PIQA (78.24→77.75) drop at 6.7B.

Comparison of the authors' law with the Liew & Kato CPT law on the same extrapolation scenarios (R² 0.934/0.982/0.979 vs 0.910/0.946/0.953). Shows predictive accuracy depends on functional-form choice.
Best model size switches with FLOPs for pretrained vs split models (compute-dependent optimal size, no power fit).

record.verdict_notes: Extrapolation spans only about 2× in parameters, so V2's orders-of-magnitude claim is untested here. Appendix G.1 notes parameter identifiability problems: very different parameter values give similar fits, so parameters are bounded. This bears on V7 but is a method remark, not a tested result. No uncertainty is reported. Internal inconsistencies: '130' test runs vs Table 1's 640, and MAE '0.6−1.5' in the text vs Table 8. Rows for the phonebook, MoE and Pile-perplexity results were rightly omitted.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests a custom loss law for split pretraining and continued pretraining, not isolated single-stage scaling in the original setup or a separate compute-only loss law.
Extrapolation is tested for the proposed split-training law on DCLM data, not for all original-source setups.

It optimizes the pretraining-versus-specialization token allocation. It does not fit power laws for optimal parameter count and token count as functions of compute, or compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann parameter/token trends.
No fixed-parameter-count comparison isolating depth, width, or other architecture details.
Tests split pretraining/CPT on text; it does not test other modalities, repeated-data scaling, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream evaluation is zero-shot QA on the listed benchmarks; it does not establish a general downstream scaling relation across tasks or training regimes.

No systematic sensitivity experiment establishes how fitted exponents or optimal allocations change with setup or fitting choices. The paper discusses identifiability and compares a different law, but does not test the version's full claim.

rows.subject: Per-domain proposed scaling-law fits
rows.operation_detail: Fit on lower CPT-token budgets and test on higher CPT-token budgets for each cluster
rows.measure: Average held-out fit metrics across domains: MAE 0.0019, MRE 0.0008, r 0.9987
rows.note: The table reports separate metrics for all 16 domains and an average; this row records the reported aggregate.
rows.check: Fixed 1.3B size; extrapolation only from CPT <20B to ≥20B tokens (CPT range about 5–30B). Train-fit r is lower for domain 15 (0.8697) and domain 8 (0.9393), but test r is ≥0.9959 for all domains.

rows.subject: Proposed split-training scaling law
rows.operation_detail: Use a custom loss function with a PT/CPT-dependent bias and power-law terms
rows.baseline: Chinchilla-type additive law described by the paper
rows.value: The proposed law adds a sigmoid bias depending on CPT tokens and model size, power terms in CPT/pretraining tokens, and a power term in model size.
rows.note: The paper says the two-stage setting requires differences in the loss functional form; it does not report fitted exponents in this passage.
rows.check: Describes the study's own law and its design desiderata, not a measured result. The need for a modified form is argued, not shown against a plain Chinchilla fit.

rows.subject: Fitted split-training scaling law
rows.operation_detail: Estimate optimal pretraining tokens as a function of total training budget
rows.measure: Optimal pretraining fraction and number of pretraining tokens
rows.value: The optimal pretraining fraction decays with budget, while the optimal number of pretraining tokens increases with budget.
rows.uncertainty: Shaded intervals in Figure 12 show allocations within 0.005 loss of the optimum.
rows.locator: Figure 4; Sections 5.3 and Appendix H, Figure 12
rows.note: The paper reports a trend but does not fit the optimal allocation as a power law of compute.
rows.check: PT-vs-CPT token allocation is a different construct from V3's N-vs-D split. Contrary to the note, Appendix G.2 does fit the optimal PT fraction as a power law in N.

relationships.condition: Split PT/CPT training on DCLM domains 0 and 8; fit on ≤1.3B and lower token budgets, tested on 2.7B and higher budgets (about 2× range)
relationships.reason: Held-out MAE is 0.009–0.025 with R² 0.934–0.982 (r1–r6). Per-domain CPT-token extrapolation averages test r 0.9987 (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Held-out MAE was 0.009–0.025 with R² of 0.934–0.982, and per-domain continual-pretraining token extrapolation averaged r=0.9987.

relationships.condition: Text continued pretraining after shared pretraining, 100M–2.7B, DCLM clusters
relationships.reason: A law with power terms in N, D and Dk fits and predicts held-out CPT-domain loss accurately (r1–r7).
relationships.display_finding: A law with power terms in model size, shared-pretraining data and domain data accurately fitted and predicted held-out continued-pretraining domain loss.

relationships.condition: Functional form in the two-stage regime
relationships.reason: From the text, not rows: the fitted law adds a sigmoid irreducible-loss term beyond Chinchilla's form. An alternative law fits worse (R² 0.910–0.953 vs 0.934–0.979, Table 7). Plain Chinchilla was not tested.
relationships.display_finding: The fitted law added a sigmoid irreducible-loss term and achieved R²=0.934–0.979 versus 0.910–0.953 for an alternative; plain Chinchilla was not tested.

relationships.condition: 1.3B models at 120/240/360B total tokens, varying PT fraction
relationships.reason: Authors state QA accuracy rises then falls around the loss-optimal split, so downstream tracks loss (r11). Weak evidence: figure only, with a coarse grid.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy rose and then fell around the loss-optimal pretraining split across the tested token budgets.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The proposed split-training loss law on the tested DCLM domains and model/token ranges
reader_labels.reason: The held-out loss fits have low MAE and high R², including held-out model sizes and token ranges (r1-r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Split pretraining/CPT rather than ordinary single-stage pretraining
reader_labels.reason: The authors use a custom PT/CPT-dependent functional form, rather than testing a standalone power law under the original setup (r8).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Held-out larger model sizes and higher PT/CPT token budgets in the proposed split-training setup
reader_labels.reason: Small-model/lower-token fits predict held-out losses with the reported MAE and R² values (r1-r6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pretraining-versus-specialization allocation for the tested split models
reader_labels.reason: The optimal pretraining fraction falls as budget rises and the token count rises, but the paper does not fit the claimed stable power laws for parameter and token counts against compute (r9-r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study finds accurate scaling predictions in this regime but uses a modified PT/CPT-dependent law; it provides no evidence for other modalities or the other listed regimes (r1-r8).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Optimal split versus same-size pretraining on the reported QA benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: The split 1.3B and 2.7B models score higher on most reported benchmark comparisons, though not all (r12-r27).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Cross-size comparisons with the pretrained 7B entry in Table 10
reader_labels.reason: The larger model is not consistently better than the split 2.7B model across benchmarks (r28-r35).
